content.text:
DnD 5.5 Ranger spells are an interesting mix of buffs and utility options
	with a handful of direct damage spells and healing options. Most of the spells
	are taken from the Druid’s spell list, though the Ranger gets several unique
	options like Hunter’s Mark and Conjure Barrage.

The Ranger’s spell selection is also limited heavily by WotC’s concepts about
	what a ranger is and where they go on adventures. Spells will heavily favor
	fighting in forests (or in forest-like environments like orchards. Basically
	anywhere with trees and other abundant foliage), which means that if you’re
	fighting anywhere else, your spell options are more limited.

The Ranger’s spellcasting runs into issues with Concentration due to the
	class’s reliance on Hunter’s Mark. Several of the Ranger’s class and subclass
	features only function while you’re using Hunter’s Mark, which means that
	casting other Concentration spells locks you out of some of your features.
	Powerful options like Summon Beast will easily beat Hunter’s Mark’s damage
	output, but you’ll need to consider any other benefits you might give up when
	you use those spells.
RPGBOT uses a color coding scheme which is simple to understand and easy to read at a glance. This system is designed to help players make informed decisions for their dnd character builds.

: Bad, useless options, or options which

: OK options, or useful options
		that only apply in rare circumstances. Useful sometimes.

: Fantastic options, often essential
		to the function of your character. Useful very frequently.

content.text: The advice in this article is based on the current
State of the 2024 DnD Character Optimization Meta

as of when the article was last updated. Keep in mind that the state of the meta periodically changes as new source materials are released, and the article will be updated accordingly as time allows. Also be sure to check for
We will not include 3rd-party content, Unearthed Arcnaa content, or homebrew in guides for official content because we can’t assume that your game will allow them.

Fighting Style (Druidic Warrior) allows you to select two Cantrips. In order
	to justify the opportunity cost of choosing Druidic Warrior over any other
	fighting style, your choice of Cantrips in the context of the rest of your
	build needs to both justify the opportunity cost and answer the question “why
	not just play a Druid?”

Since Cantrips reduce your reliance on Strength or Dexterity, we’ll assume
	that you’re maximizing Charisma rather than Strength or Dexterity and building
	around using cantrips instead of using weapons normally.

items.text:
: Good damage and cheap area control, but it requires Concentration, and
		it’s not good enough to justify over concentrating on Hunter’s Mark.
: Very flavorful, but almost totally useless.

: Low damage for a cantrip (d6-based), but the big appeal is Disadvantage
		on the target’s next weapon attack. Unfortunately, it works on Constitution
		saving throws, and those tend to be relatively high compared to other saving
		throws.
: Really good, but you likely can’t make room for it.
: This spell is almost totally useless.

: The forced movement is the main appeal, and you can get that from Weapon
		Mastery much more reliably.

: 1d6+Wis damage. You get Extra Attack, and this doesn’t consume
		Concentration, so it can work with Hunter’s Mark. You can also fire the
		stones from a sling to use Weapon Mastery. The biggest issue is spending a
		Bonus Action every 3 shots, which will compete heavily with Hunter’s Mark.
		It’s doable, but there will be turns where you won’t have Hunter’s Mark in
		place because you needed to refresh Magic Stone.

: Situational. Use this to send messages without revealing your
		position.

: You know what else can do this? A shovel. Sure, shoveling will take a
		long time, but you get at most 3 Cantrips (5 with Circle of the Land), and
		if you can replace a Cantrip with a mundane item it’s probably a bad
		Cantrip. The only important function is to create difficult terrain, but
		you’re limited to two ongoing effects, which means you only get two 5-foot
		squares. And, again, you could do that with a shovel. You’re about as likely
		to use this in combat as you are to use a shovel, too.

: This highest damage die for Cantrips, at least until Toll the Dead came
		along. Poison spray has serious problems: 10 ft. range, and it works on a
		Constitution saving throw, so enemies will frequently resist it.

: Shillelagh will be more effective, so get Shillelagh unless you
		desperately need an empty hand for some reason.

: A decent attack Cantrip, it notably also allows you to hold the flame and
		carry it around as a light source. The action economy is annoying, though:
		you need to spend a Bonus Action to activate the spell, then an Action to
		actually attack. You could walk around with this running to keep it ready,
		but there’s not much reason to do when Starry Wisp exists.

: Considerably more difficult to use than Guidance. Your best bet is to
		throw this on an ally before going into combat, but if you have that luxury
		you should be casting a better Concentration spell.
for more on how great Shape Water is.

: Basically the reason Druidic Warrior exists. In a lot of ways, this
		cantrip perfectly exemplifies the trade you’re making with Druidic Warrior.
		You get to turn a club or quarterstaff into a longsword equivalent using
		your Wisdom modifier. Consider grabbing Polearm Master, too.

: The only benefit to Spare the Dying is that it has 15-foot range, and
		that’s so little range that it’s hardly worth considering. Buy a Healer’s
		Kit and walk the 15 feet if you need to stabilize an ally as an Action.

: Decent damage, good damage type, and it prevents enemies from hiding or
		turning invisibile. But it won’t keep up with other options since you get
		Extra Attack.

: The damage is fine, but the real appeal is the pull effect. 10 feet may
		not seem like much, but its enough to pull enemies off of ledges, to pull
		low-flying enemies into melee, to pull enemies into an area control effect
		like Create Bonfire or Wall of Fire, to pull enemies out of a grapple, or in
		a pinch you can pull an ally out of a dangerous location (albeit at the
		price of some friendly fire).

: Damaging every creature within 5 feet of you is great if you’re in melee
		facing numerous enemies. Even with Extra Attack you will deal more damage
		with this against three or more foes than you could with a weapon. See our
		article on

for a breakdown of the math comparing melee Cantrips to normal martial
		attacks.

: You get spellcasting later and slower than anyone else, so you have very
		few options for protecting yourself from non-weapon damage. This will handle
		that issue, but it will eat your spell slots quickly so be sure to eliminate
		the source of the elemental damage as quickly as possible so that you don’t
		run through your spell slots too quickly.

The biggest challenge for Absorb Elements is that is has Somatic
			components, which require a free hand. By default, this means that
			two-weapon fighting builds and sword-and-board builds will be unable to
			use this unless you’re dilligent about drawing and stowing your weapon,
			which both makes opportunity attacks hard and only allows Absorb Elements
			every other round. Unfortunately, the only way around this is
: Great to cast as a Ritual when you’re resting, but .

: Arguably easier than proficiency in Animal Handling, but it will become
		obsolete once beasts disappear around CR 10.

: Largely useless. Even for Beast Master Rangers, your beast has 8
		Intelligence, so it doesn’t qualify.

: Long
		range, no save, and it inhibits stealth, Perception, and Concentration. It’s
		somehow both broadly useful but also very difficult to justify.

Buzzing Bee prevents the target from benefiting from invisibility, which
			means that they can’t benefit from hiding. But you need to be able to see
			them, which means that most enemies that rely on invisiblity won’t care.
			This doesn’t allow a save like Faerie Fire does, but Faerie Fire also
			don’t require you to see the target, and Faerie Fire also works as a great
			support option even when enemies aren’t invisibile.

Imposing Disadvantage on Perception may be helpful for sneaking past
			enemies, but since Buzzing Bee is single-target and has a Verbal
			component, which makes it difficult to use in most stealth situations.

The Concentration option may be helpful against enemy spellcasters, but
			for the same action cost and spell slot you can use any number of other
			spells that could actually break Concentration.

: Rangers don’t have as many spell slots as a full caster, so using your
		precious few slots on healing can be difficult. However, someone in the
		party needs to be able to heal the primary healer if they fall unconscious,
		and you’re someone.

: Ideally someone in the party who can cast more spells than you will
		handle this, but sometimes you don’t really have a choice. Fortunately, you
		can cast it as a Ritual to avoid spending precious spell slots.

: Very situational, and unless you can also cast Protection From Poison,
		there’s little you can do about it anyway other than physically avoiding the
		threat. Fortunately, this can be cast as a Ritual.

: Almost exclusive to Rangers, Ensnaring Strike is a great way to handle
		single targets that are causing you problems, especially if the target is a
		melee monster. Note that you can use this at range, so archery builds can
		ensnare a target, then either wear them down or shift their attention to
		other foes.

It’s a Strength save, which means that most spellcasters and many agile
			enemies will have trouble with it, but big melee brutes will probably
			resist it. After the initial save, it takes an Action and and a Strength
			(Athletics) check (not a save) to escape, and the target takes damage
			every round, so they’ll likely want to escape quickly. The damage scales
			linearly with spell level, so this remains a powerful and efficient use of
			a spell slot throughout your career, but restraining the target is much
			more impactful than the damage itself.

Ensnaring Strike is also an excellent counter to flying enemies because
			being restrained causes creatures which fly nonmagically to fall, which
			means that if you shoot a griffon or something it’s going to take a pile
			of falling damage.

: A great area control spell at any level. Strength saving throws tend to
		be low for any creature that isn’t a gigantic Strength-based brute, so it’s
		easy to restrain even high-level enemies. However, it requires Concentration
		so you can’t easily combine it with things like Hunter’s Mark.

: An excellent way to cover your escape, but you can’t see through the fog
		any better than anyone else, so don’t expect to fight in this without some
		other advantage most of the time. Fog Cloud can be a way to negate Advantage
		if your enemies have the upper hand, so if you’re facing enemies who are
		invisible, hidden, or have some other source of Advantage, Fog Cloud can
		take that away, effectively leveling the playing field so that no one can
		see each other. Such situations are rare, but it’s nice to know that there’s
		a countermeasure when those situations do arise.

: An excellent resource, both in terms of healing and utility. A Druid can
		usually spare a prepared spell so that they can dump spells into Goodberry
		at the end of the day, but that may be harder for a Ranger since you get
		such a small number of spells known. Still, dumping your spell slots into a
		pile of goodberries the day before you leave on an adventure will give you a
		helpful pad of hit points that you can quickly use to heal after combat
		without resorting to a short rest.

: This shouldn’t be a go-to option, but it’s a nice way to handle
		tightly-packed groups of weak foes. Just don’t rely on it too heavily, as it
		will eat your spell slots quickly without a big payoff.

: The Ranger’s bread and butter, and required to benefit from many of the
		Ranger’s class and subclass features. Many rangers will spend the bulk of
		their time using Concentration on Hunter’s Mark while they focus upon single
		foes before switching to the next foe. As a Ranger, your Favored Enemy
		feature gets you a pool of free castings of Hunter’s Mark, which allows you
		to save your spell slots for other things without losing chunks of your
		class.

Hunter’s Mark taking so much focus in the design of the DnD 5.5 Ranger is
			a significant pain point in the class’s design. Unfortunately, there isn’t
			a way around it without giving up class and subclass features, though not
			all subclasses require Hunter’s Mark to the same degree. As you gain
			levels, you may find that other Concentration spells like Elemental Weapon
			and Summon Beast are more impactful uses for your Concentration.

: A great
		boost to your mobility with a Bonus Action casting time. You can’t afford to
		use this in every encounter, but it’s great if you need to get past
		obstacles or hazards.

: A
		helpful buff for highly-mobile characters, and with an hour-long duration it
		can be a great use of low-level spell slots once your 1st-level spells start
		lagging in combat.

: Good
		for setting a trap, or if you’re resting somewhere dangerous with a
		convenient choke point like a narrow hallway. Targets are restrained for at
		least one round, which is hopefully enough for you to fight your way out of
		your bedroll and grab a weapon.

:
		Situational, but sometimes the only witnesses are wild animals and you just
		need a clue from your local family of squirrels. Fortunately, you can cast
		it as a Ritual, so it won’t cut into your spell slots.

: Cast it as a Bonus Action, and you get the benefits of Disengage for the
		duration of the spell. You can also end the spell early for a boost of speed
		and a singled buffed attack.

If you’re built to fight at range and something gets uncomfortably close
			to you, turn this on, step back 5 ft., shoot it to express your distaste,
			then run away.

: With an 8-hour duration and three targets, this is a staple buff that’s
		worth casting literally every day. Keep in mind that this actually increases
		the targets’ hit point maximum, so temporary hit points can be added, too.

Aid’s casting time allows it to be used in combat, which is unusual but
			offers an interesting option. With three targets and a 30-foot range, you
			can cast it to both buff and heal your allies during combat. Targets’
			current hit points and hit point maximum both increase, so allies at 0 hit
			points are healed in addition to having their hit point maximum raised,
			thereby allowing Aid to serve a similar function to Mass Healing Word.

However, since spells don’t stack with themselves, it’s hard to repeat
			this trick. You’ll need to cast Aid again using higher-level spell slots,
			which can get expensive quickly, so Mass Healing Word is probably better
			if Aid is already running and if Mass Healing Word is an option for your
			party.

: Only
		situationally useful, but the 24-hour duration means that you can cast it
		before a Long Rest and still enjoy the effect all day.

: Situational and
		less reliable than similar spells like Sending, but it’s also a spell level
		lower than Sending and it’s a Ritual. If you know that your recipient is
		going to be wherever you send your message, this works fine. Unfortunately,
		the recipient doesn’t get to respond.

: The best
		AC that the Druid can get until you can afford half plate or you get to 20
		Dexterity. Not essential, and it will become obsolete, but it may be a
		useful AC buff depending on your stats.

: The
		intent is that you will use this to scout an area using an animal. Maybe you
		cast Speak With Animals on it, then send it to explore somewhere and use
		Beast Sense to get a first-hand account. If you’re desperate, you might also
		use this on an animal and carry it around to help address issues like
		blindness, deafness, or your own lack of Darkvision. Your DM might
		reasonably impose Disadvantage on things like attack rolls when doing this
		due to the uncomfortable shift in perspective, but if you’re truly desperate
		it might be enough.

: With a
		1-action casting time you might actually be able to use this in combat, but
		the damage is really low (compare 1d6+Dex twice with Extra Attack to a total
		of 4d6 from Cordon of Arrows), so the intent is clearly to use this to lay
		ambushes or to protect an area where you’re resting. Unlike similar options
		like Alarm and Snare, this doesn’t make a significant amount of noise when
		it goes into effect, so consider tying a bell to each piece of ammunition
		after you cast the spell so that you now when it’s triggered.

There’s nothing preventing you from casting this multiple times, but the
			rules for stacking may disallow you from casting it in the same space
			multiple times. If you have a bunch of spell slots before you take a Long
			Rest, you could spend them on Cordon of Arrows to create an exceptionally
			dangerous area for intruders. Unfortunately, there’s no way to exclude
			your allies from this or to end the spell early, so be careful not to let
			allies stumble through the area.

:
		Fantastic at any level. 8-hour duration, no Concentration, and almost
		nothing in the game can match 150 feet of Darkvision. If you can afford the
		spell slots, cast this on everyone in the party who doesn’t get it from
		their race.

: More
		plot point than actual spell, this will rarely see use by players in a
		typical campaign. Used as intended, this creates a small area in which two
		characters can kick each other in the shins until someone runs out of hit
		points without risk of anyone actualy dying. But it doesn’t do anything
		about other nasty effects, so participants can petrify, curse, or otherwise
		ruin their opponent’s day without Dueling Ground protecting them.

Dueling Ground’s fighting ring is notably porous. The participants are
			free to interact with anything outside of the ring unless they leave it,
			and even then the spell doesn’t actually end. If you can bring this up in
			time for combat, you can effectively give both participants Death Ward for
			the spell’s duration (or until a third creature enters the area).

:
		Fantastic and versatile. Using this to buff Charisma for your party’s Face
		will make any social situation go a lot better.

: Too
		expensive and too imprecise. Invest in Investigation.

:
		Potentially a great way to shove enemies around, but at 15 ft. per round
		enemies will frequently be able to walk back the distance they were pushed
		without issue. Your best bet is to push enemies into area control effects,
		but since Gust of Wind requires your Concentration you may have trouble
		creating effects to use.

: Likely
		not good enough to replace healing from a Short Rest when your party is in
		rough shape, but very efficient for the spell slot if your Wisdom modifier
		is high. It’s not nearly as fast as Cure Wounds and requires Concentration,
		so it’s not great in combat, but it’s decent between fights if you don’t
		have time to rest.

The total healing goes up by 1d6 times your spellcasting modifier per
			spell level past level 2, so you can double the healing by using a level 3
			slot. That’s better scaling than Cure Wounds, but remember that you’re
			trading time for the extra healing per spell slot.

:
		Situational, but a situation that comes up often.

: Too situational,
		and too easy to counter. Anyone with any knowledge of magic that’s trying to
		hide something will wrap it in lead.

: If your
		game uses magic items, you may never need this. If it doesn’t, this is
		essential. A bonus to your attacks makes your damage output multiplicatively
		more reliable. With a 1-hour duration and no Concentration, one casting
		provides a lot of value from one of your few spell slots.

: A +10
		bonus in a game where most characters max out at +11 is huge. The bonus is
		enough to offset problems like a fighter in full plate armor. But remember:
		this is not invisibility. You can’t cast this and crouch down in plain view
		and magically disappear. I hear that mistake being made constantly on
		podcasts. A +10 bonus doesn’t negate line of sight rules. You still need
		cover or something.

:
		Situational, but poison is common across the full CR range, so this is a
		fantastic defensive option at any level. The 1-hour duration means that you
		can get a lot of mileage out of a single spell slot even if you cast it
		ahead of time.

: Verbal components
		are extremely common in spells, including many that spellcasters frequently
		use to escape dangerous situations. If you can trap an enemy spellcaster in
		place (such as by having an ally grapple them) and drop Silence around them,
		you’ll significantly limit their options. In the 2024 rules, spellcasting
		enemies will have combat actions that aren’t actually spells and which will
		ignore Silence, but you’ll still limit some of their best options.

, and it’s every time the creature “travels”,
		not every time the creature moves. So if you push or pull the creature, they
		take damage. A 20-foot radius spread is a fairly large area, too, so you can
		easily affect whole rooms or long stretches of hallway.

: The
		lowest-level Summon spell. With a 1-hour duration you can get a ton of
		mileage out of a spell slot, and the beasts are very effective in combat. If
		you have other melee allies, throwing one of the beasts with Pack Tactics
		alongside them can yield a lot of consistent, reliable damage. The Air beast
		has Flyby, which is appealing if you need a more durable version of the owl
		familiar’s hit-and-run Help trick, but won’t be as effective offensively as
		the Land and Water options.

Summon Beast has an odd place in the Ranger’s tactics. It competes for
			your Concentration with Hunter’s Mark, but the beast deals 1d8+6 (avg.
			10.5) damage per turn with a level 2 spell slot. Hunter’s Mark, assuming
			two attacks, deals 2d6 (avg. 7). Summon Beast also puts a body on the
			field to take damage in place of the actual party mmbers. In most cases, a
			summon is a better use of a spell slot than HUnter’s Mark, which is
			especially frustrating because many of the Ranger’s class and subclass
			features requirey ou to have Hunter’s Mark running.

: Only
		situationally useful. If you need an ally to block a choke point, this could
		be a helpful defensive boost. Otherwise, characters typically want the
		mobility to respond to problems, and the +1 AC isn’t worth Concentration.
		Strongly consider Barkskin before casting this.

: Bonus
		Action casting time, and the damage doesn’t allow a save. This is similar in
		concept to Zephyr Strike, but you get free damage in exchange for a
		considerably higher spell level. The damage may not be huge by this level,
		but in encounters with numerous enemies this can add up quickly.

:
		Portable, good damage, and a 10-minute duration. The pack of animals is 10
		feet across and the damage effect extends 10 feet from the pack, so the area
		is a square that’s 30 feet across. You move the area without spending any
		sort of action, so you can still use the rest of your action economy for
		other cool stuff.

Much like Summon Beast, Conjure Animals has a weird place in the Ranger’s
			tactics. It doesn’t last as long, but the 3d10 damage will easily exceed
			Hunter’s Mark, especially when facing multiple enemies.

: A
		massive 60-foot cone, a great damage type, and decent damage. It won’t deal
		as much total damage as Conjure Animals over the course of a fight, but it’s
		good burst damage if you catch a bunch of enemies clustered close
		together.

: A
		Continual Flame, Light, or even a torch is typically sufficient, but
		sometimes you need to light up larger areas like dark battlefields or
		massive caverns. This also dispels magical darkness of 3rd level or lower,
		which is great if you’re fighting enemies like drow which can produce
		magical darkness. Since it produces sunlight, you can use this offensively
		against enemies like vampires and enemies Sunlight Sensitivity like
		drow.

: Every
		party needs someone who can cast Dispel Magic. It’s simply too important to
		forgo.

: Not
		significantly better than Magic Weapon, a spell level higher, and it takes
		Concentration. Unfortunately, you can’t use both. Instead, you can cast
		Magic Weapon and Hunter’s Mark to get the same attack bonus and more
		additional damage.

:
		This is a waste of a spell slot. It amounts to at most 12d6 damage, which is
		a tragic waste of a 3rd-level spell slot. If you somehow manage to hit one
		target with all 12 arrows, you’ll do more damage than Fireball. But you have
		to somehow hit with a bunch of arrows or pass them off to someone who will,
		and following the typical attack vs. AC progression means that a player will
		hit something like 65% of the time, which means you’re getting 65% of the
		maximum damage, so something like 7d6. At that point, Erupting Earth is
		better.

:
		Basically a better version of Hail of Thorns, but the damage is rarely good
		enough to justify the spell slot so save this for when you have a big group
		of enemies in a small area. 5 or more seems like a good number.

: Good,
		but not totally essential. Divination spells include things like See
		Invisibility, so if you or your party relies on invisibility of any kind
		this protects from several magical countermeasures to both stealth and
		invisibility. However, most enemies aren’t spellcasters and won’t have
		access to those divination options, so you can’t justify casting this every
		day. The spell also has an expensive material component specifically to
		deter you from casting this all the time. Still, with an 8-hour duration, if
		you need this spell it’s going to do exactly what you need it to do.

: Situational.
		Outside of normal adventuring activities, the ability to enrich land to
		double crop yields is very useful. But DnD is a game primarily about
		adventuring, and the option to make an area of plants overgrown is the more
		important option for most adventurers. In most cases, Entangle will work
		fine if you just need to slow your enemies down, but Plant Growth doesn’t
		expire, so those plants remain difficult to walk through until someone
		clears the plants (which may requires hours of chopping and/or burning). The
		spell also doesn’t specify that the plants grow along the ground or
		surfaces, so RAW it can create a sphere of plants, creating super-difficult
		terrain extending 100 feet into the air, potentially engulfing flying
		enemies.

The math on Plant Growth’s speed reduction is impressive. Since most
			creatures have a speed of around 30 feet, moving at 1/4 speed means that
			they can move one 5-foot square and be left with 10 feet of movement that
			won’t get them anywhere (unless they dash or something). Jeremy Crawford
			has clarified that Plant Growth

, so it’s possible that difficult terrain would stack with Plant Growth,
			but I personally think that’s not how it’s intended to work. Plant Growth
			specifies that “a creature moving through the area must spend 4 feet of
			movement for every 1 foot” while the difficult terrain rule specifies that
			“moving 1 foot in difficult terrain costs 2 feet of speed”, and since
			those two statements conflict I think you’re intended to use whichever
			effect is greater rather than stacking them or multiplying them or
			something.

While it’s not discussed in the text of the spell, it seems likely that
			Plant Growth would also impede vision. If you turn a nicely-tended hedge
			into a 100-foot-radius hemisphere of super-difficult terrain, there’s
			clearly enough stuff in the way that seeing through it is difficult. This
			would necessarily mean that creatures inside the area would likely be
			concealed to some degree, so don’t expect to drop Plant Growth on an enemy
			and then spend the next several turns spraying them with cantrips until
			they fall down.

Plant Growth’s problematic limitation is that it requires plants to be in
			the area. However, there doesn’t seem to be any restriction on how many or
			how large these plants must be (just that they must be “normal”, whatever
			that means), and where there’s lack of clarity there’s room for
			shenanigans. For example: you might carry around a potted plant and throw
			it into the area to provide the necessary plant life to support the spell.
			Plants like mint or clover can fit into a small pot, and when you make
			them grow you get a pretty and pleasant-smelling field of super-difficult
			terrain. If your DM scoffs at the idea of 100-foot-tall clover patches,
			consider carrying a bonsai tree or some other plant which would normally
			be very tall (though a bonsai might not qualify as “normal” since we don’t
			know what that word means here).

: An
		important, staple defensive option, but it’s single-target and requires
		Concentration, so you can’t afford to keep it running constantly.

:
		Everyone who is capable of casting this should keep it handy. It’s simply
		too good to forgo.

: Situational. If you
		encounter plant creatures, this may allow you to handle them
		nonviolently.

: The
		summon options do little to improve upon Summon Beast.

:
		Situational, but crucial when you need it. Fortunately, it’s a Ritual, so it
		should never eat a spell slot.

: Usually
		flight is a better option than walking across a liquid. This can be cast as
		a Ritual, but it’s not useful often enough to prepare it if you don’t know
		for sure

:
		Fantastic for melee builds. Area damage in an Emanation. Conjure Woodland
		Beings Disengage as a Bonus Action so that you can easily move between
		targets without provoking Opportunity Attacks, and your Action is still
		available for attacking once the spell is running.

Ranged builds could use similar tactics, but you may prefer to remain at
			a safer distance. Conjure Beasts may also be a better choice because you
			can move it from a comfortable distance, though it will deal less damage
			than Conjure Woodland Beings.

: By the time you can
		cast this, beasts have stopped being a threat.

: Put the
		vine on a ceiling and use it to haul a creature off the ground. If they
		break the grapple, they fall and take damage, then you can grab them again.
		If they stay still, you and your party have an easy target that can’t run
		away. If your party can place an inexpensive ongoing damage effect like
		Create Bonfire, you can step behind cover and wait. Upcasting the spell
		allows you to target more creatures, keeping this relevant at any level
		against any Huge or smaller enemy that struggles to fight at range.

: This is
		a challenging spell. The benefits are great, but the duration is short and
		the spell’s effectiveness depends heavily on how you’re built. Primal Beast
		is clearly intended to be the scary offensive form, but a druid making
		Strength-based melee attacks is either a poorly built druid or they’re using
		Wild Shape.

Great Tree is usually the better option: advantage on Dexterity- and
			Wisdom-based attacks covers important options like daggers, but also
			covers anything you can use with Shillelagh. The temporary hit points will
			help compensate for your poor AC, and the area of difficult terrain will
			help you keep enemies in convenient melee range.

Circle of the Moon Druids can get some use out of Primal Beast, but it
			has a Bonus Action casting time and a 1-minute duration, so until you get
			Beast Spells at 18th level it’s hard to get both effects going at the same
			time and you have at most 9 rounds to actually use the effects. Circle of
			the Moon can choose to Wild Shape as either an Action or a Bonus Action so
			you can start both effects in the turn, but you won’t be able to do much
			else in that turn. During the remaining 9 rounds you’ll be very effective,
			but it’s still only 9 rounds.

: More
		effective than mundane tracking, but the 1,000-foot range can be a problem
		if the target is actively fleeing from you. If you’re going to use this, be
		sure that you’re moving faster than your target.

: This
		is effectively a summoning spell which summons 4 CR 1/8 creatures. By the
		time you can cast this, that’s utterly useless. The best-case scenario is
		using this on wooden items that enemies are carrying. You can’t use it on
		magic items, so you can’t use it on the enemy wizard’s magic staff, but you
		can use it on mundane enemy weapons like spears. Most enemies use nonmagical
		weapons even if their attacks are magic, so this could be occasionally
		useful through the whole level range. But that depends on your enemies’
		weapon selection, which is difficult to predict, so this is only
		situationally useful.

: If you
		just need a body in a fight, or if you need a creature that can burrow, this
		is great. Otherwise, you may find Summon Beast or Giant Insect to be more
		effective.

: This is a good spell, but you get exactly one level 5 spell slot, and
		this is too situational to sit on your best spell slot hoping for this to
		matter.

: 3 miles
		isn’t an especially large range, but since this a ritual you can cast this
		repeatedly as you travel. You might get some useful information, but your DM
		(and your party) might get sick of sitting around waiting for you to perform
		the ritual every time you travel 6 miles. You might be able to get away with
		performing this from the back of a wagon or something, which would let you
		cast it repeatedly without slowing things down.

: Unlike
		a typical summon spell, this conjures an immobile elemental that restrains
		your enemies. It might be effective if the elemental can reach everywhere
		within a room, or if you need to hold a choke point for an extended period,
		but otherwise you’ll do better with other area control spells.

: Decent damage and a good damage type. This is the closest that the Ranger
		gets to casting Fireball. If you can hit a crowd of targets, it’s worth the
		spell slot even if they pass the saves. The damage is also 1d8 higher than
		Conjure Barrage cast at the same level, and can be cast from a much safer
		distance. Unfortunately, full casters can deal considerably more damage by
		this level, so it will feel underwheling compared to Wizards slinging Meteor
		Swarm at the same level.

(Optional): A crucial
		healing option, but if your party has survived long enough to reach this
		level you almost certainly have access to this already, and you shouldn’t
		need to learn it permanently.

: If you have 20 Wisdom,
		your Spell Attacks are as good as a full caster, which makes this great
		burst damage. But remember that Rangers only get one level 5 spell slot, so
		save this for when you can hit a bunch of targets.

: A bad
		summoning spell compared to other options on your list. You can’t justify
		using your single level 5 spell slot on this.

: Hugely improves your
		action economy, but since it requires Concentration, you can’t combine it
		with Hunter’s Mark or most other damage boosts, and it requires a ranged
		weapon with ammunition, so thrown weapon builds will find no value here. The
		ideal is to use this with an archery build, have Magic Weapon running, then
		turn this on in an important fight.

Consider a same ranger with a longbow and without Crossbow Expert. For
			that ranger, two extra attacks doubles their number of attacks for the
			turn, taking their damage output from 2d8+2d6+10 with Hunter’s Mark (avg.
			26) to 4d8+20 (avg. 38), a nearly 50% increase in damage output. We’re
			again ignoring the possibility of critical hits, fighting style, magic
			items, etc. but any of those things tip the math further in favor of Swift
			Quiver. Even if you’re built for melee, Swift Quiver is a great way to
			switch to ranged combat and deal a bunch of damage.

Now consider a high-level ranger with Crossbow Expert, nonmagical hand
			crossbows, and 20 Dexterity. 4 attacks will deal a total of 4d6+20 (avg.
			36), while three attacks with Hunter’s Mark running will deal 6d6+15 (avg.
			36). There is some nuance to the math because the extra attack means
			another chance to score a critical hit, but the difference isn’t big
			enough to make Swift Quiver worth being a level 5 spell when you can cast
			Hunter’s Mark as a 1st-level spell.

Magic weapons, feats, or class features which add additional damage will
			make the math favor Swift Quiver more heavily, but I’m not sure how much
			you would need to justify the difference in spell level between Hunter’s
			Mark and Swift Quiver.

: In a
		forest this can be a helpful way to quickly travel short distances, but It’s
		not nearly as effective for short distances as Misty Step, it’s not good for
		long distances (you can go about a mile total if all the trees line up
		perfectly and you run a little bit during your turns), and you’re totally
		limited by the position and species of trees.

: This
		would be a great spell if you could guarantee that you were in an area with
		trees, grass, and loose stones every time you fought something. But you
		can’t do that, and forests are a relatively small portion of most worlds’
		environments.
